chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
title: Pay in 1926 and civil service afterwards
summary: Dance and Caldwell compare 1926 wages with later pay; Caldwell joined civil service after the war and ran a duplicating room at City College.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: You know. But the thing that sort of surprised me was, you know, I always thought about when Duke Pete was at the Cotton Club, that was a great thing.
And of course that did make his name. But then I mean -- different times I found out that, sure, that was a very prestigious job, but they were underpaid there.
And I -- but, nevertheless, what you were earning in those days -- I mean it would sound like nothing today, but it wasn't bad money compared with what you'd be doing anything else, was it?
No, it wasn't. When we were down there with Charlie, and Duke was up there -- went into the Cotton Club, I started with Benny what he was paying up there. For instance, my --
Well, you couldn't have -- I mean if you quit music and you'd gone into a factory or something, well, you couldn't have earned what you earned with Charlie, could you?

No. Until recently, until after the war, World War II, a lot of musicians got tired of the road like I did and started taking civil service exams. See? Lot of them became tellers in the banks, I became charge of the Duplicating Room King over at New York City College. And then you get on the civil service list. You start off with a basic salary, say, of $2,700.00 a year, and wind up, ten years, making about $5,700.00, close, as the thing goes along. The economy was and rent going up. Price of food was (unintelligible). So you join in naturally with the civil service, and that's it. You had to go up with it. So that's the way it was.
Yeah, I mean, you know, $25.00 a week in 1926 would put you up -- be worth about 500.00 today.
Today, yeah. When we went on there man with Charlie, we was getting $75.00 a (unintelligible).
And there wasn't no taxes then.
So, like I say, $75.00 then were equal to around $300.00 a week now, because everything was cheaper.
